procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 15, 1967 of the Patna High Court in Crl. W.J.C. No. 92 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant approached the High Court of Patna in Cr. W.J.C. No, 92 of 1966 under Art. 226 of the Constitution and s. 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for a writ or order in the nature of habeas corpus directing his release from detention. A Bench of that High Court consisting of the learned Chief Justice and B. N. Jha J., refused to entertain that petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the Patna High Court's order.

directions: The appellant is directed to be set at liberty forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether a detention order can be justified on the basis of the remaining grounds if some of the grounds supplied are found to be vague, irrelevant, or non-existent.

law.law_text: The detention of a person is based on the 'subjective satisfaction' of the detaining authority, which must be properly based on all the reasons on which it purports to be based.

Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, a person detained is entitled to be supplied with grounds that are not vague or indefinite, enabling them to make a real and effective representation against the detention.
This constitutional requirement that grounds must not be vague must be satisfied with respect to each of the grounds communicated to the detained person.

application.application_text: The Court rejected the State's argument that a detention order could be justified on the remaining valid grounds if some were found to be defective. The Court reasoned that it is impossible to know what the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority would have been if the invalid grounds were excluded.

If some of the reasons are found to be non-existent or irrelevant, the court cannot predict whether the authority would have still been satisfied and issued the order. The court must be satisfied that the vague or irrelevant grounds, if excluded, might reasonably have affected the authority's decision.
To uphold the detention order based only on the valid grounds would be to substitute the objective standards of the court for the subjective satisfaction of the authority, which is not permissible.

Therefore, if even one of the grounds is found to be vague, irrelevant, or non-existent, it vitiates the entire detention order, as the detention is not in accordance with the procedure established by law.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a detention order cannot be sustained if any of the grounds supplied are found to be vague, irrelevant, or non-existent. The presence of even one such defective ground is sufficient to vitiate the entire order, as it is impossible to determine to what extent it influenced the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.

issue.issue_text: Whether the constitutional requirement that the grounds for detention must not be vague must be satisfied with respect to each of the grounds communicated to the person detained.

law.law_text: Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, a person detained is entitled to be communicated the grounds of their detention and to be furnished with particulars that are full and adequate enough to enable them to make a representation against the detention order.
Preventive detention is based on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority, not on an objective judicial test.

application.reasoning_text: The Court reasoned that the constitutional requirement that grounds for detention must not be vague must apply to each and every ground provided to the detained person.

If even one of the grounds is found to be vague, non-existent, or irrelevant, the entire detention order is vitiated and becomes illegal. The Court explicitly rejected the argument that a detention order could be sustained on the remaining valid grounds.

The justification for this strict rule is that the detention order is based on the 'subjective satisfaction' of the detaining authority. A court cannot speculate on what the authority's decision would have been if the invalid ground had been excluded. It is impossible to know if the invalid grounds influenced the authority's decision.
To uphold the detention based only on the valid grounds would be to substitute the court's objective judgment for the authority's subjective satisfaction, which is not permissible under the law.
Furthermore, a vague ground prevents the detained person from making an effective representation against it, thus violating a fundamental procedural safeguard guaranteed by the Constitution.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the constitutional requirement for non-vague grounds must be satisfied with respect to each individual ground communicated to the detained person. If any single ground is found to be vague, the entire detention order is considered unlawful and must be invalidated, regardless of the validity of the other grounds.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a detention order can be justified on the basis of the remaining grounds if some of the grounds supplied are found to be vague, irrelevant, or non-existent.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's detention is illegal if any one of the grounds supplied is vague or non-existent, and therefore the entire order cannot be sustained.
respondent_arguments: Even if some grounds (specifically (a) and (d)) are ignored, the detention can still be justified on the basis of the remaining grounds mentioned in the order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the constitutional requirement that the grounds for detention must not be vague must be satisfied with respect to each of the grounds communicated to the person detained.
appellant_arguments: Each one of the grounds supplied in support of the detention order must be valid; if any ground is vague, irrelevant, or non-existent, the entire detention order is illegal.
respondent_arguments: The detention order as a whole can be justified on the remaining valid grounds, even if some of the grounds are defective.

cases.case_name: Dr. Ram Krishan Bhardwaj v. State of Delhi
cases.principle: The constitutional requirement that grounds for detention must not be vague must be satisfied for each ground, and where one of the grounds is vague, the detention is illegal, even if other grounds are not vague.

cases.case_name: Shibban Lal Saksena v. State of U.P.
cases.principle: If one of the grounds for detention is found to be non-existent, irrelevant, or illusory, the entire detention order is vitiated, as it is not for the court to substitute its objective test for the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority.

cases.case_name: Dwarka Dass Bhatia v. State of Jammu and Kashmir
cases.principle: The detention order is vitiated if one of the grounds is vague or irrelevant.

cases.case_name: Rameshwar Lal Patwari v. State of Bihar
cases.principle: The detention order is vitiated if one of the grounds is vague or irrelevant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A detention order is illegal in its entirety if any one of the grounds provided is vague, non-existent, or irrelevant. The order cannot be sustained on the remaining valid grounds, as it is impossible for a court to determine whether the invalid ground influenced the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.
obiter: Individual liberty is a cherished right, and the safeguards provided by the Constitution against the improper exercise of power must be jealously watched and enforced by the Court.
Authorities cannot deal with the liberty of the individual in a casual manner, as continued indifference to individual liberty is bound to erode the structure of a democratic society.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority must be properly based on all the reasons on which it purports to be based. If some out of those reasons are found to be non-existent or irrelevant, the court cannot predicate what the subjective satisfaction of the authority would have been on the exclusion of those reasons. To uphold the order on the remaining reasons would be to substitute the objective standards of the court for the subjective satisfaction of the authority.
legal_tests_applied: The constitutional requirement that the grounds must not be vague must be satisfied with respect to each of the grounds communicated to the person detained subject to the claim of privilege under cl. { 6) of Art. 22 of the Constitution, and where one of the grounds mentioned is vague, even though the other grounds are not vague the detention is not in accordance with the procedure ·established by law and is therefore illegal.
The Court must, .however, be satisfied that ihe vague or irrelevant grounds are such as, if excluded, might reasonably have affected the subjective satisfaction of the authority.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the detention could be justified on the remaining valid grounds was rejected as 'wholly untenable'.

The court cannot determine what the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority would have been if the non-existent or irrelevant grounds were excluded. Upholding the order on the remaining grounds would substitute the court's objective standards for the authority's subjective satisfaction.
The court found that at least two of the grounds were defective: ground (a) was found to be 'vague as well as irrelevant' and ground (d) was 'non-existing'.
Based on precedent, if one of the grounds is vague, non-existent, or irrelevant, the entire detention order is vitiated and illegal, as it is not in accordance with the procedure established by law.
policy_considerations: Individual liberty is a cherished right, one of the most valuable fundamental rights guaranteed by our Constitution to the citizens of this country. If that right is invaded, excepting strictly in accordance with law, the aggrieved party is entitled to appeal to the judicial power of the State for relief.
The power given to the State under the Act is an extraordinary power. It is exercisable under special conditions and is subject io definite lirilltations.
